newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Economists say Sweden '96 borrowing data positive.
newsitem.headline: Economists say Sweden '96 borrowing data positive.

text.p: Sweden's state borrowing requirement figures released on Thursday were no surprise to the market but a lower-than-forecast figure for 1996 confirmed a rosier picture of state finances, economists said.
"The 1996 figures are important for interest rates as they confirm the radical improvement of state finances," Bengt Hansson, senior economist at Handelsbanken, told Reuters.

The central government borrowing requirement amounted to 21.0 billion crowns in 1996, which was 117.5 billion crowns lower than in 1995 and 4.6 billion crowns lower than in a forecast published last month, the National Debt Office said.
The office attributed the improvement almost entirely to a reduction in net lending as a result of early repayment of loans by state-owned companies.
Although some economists found the figures a bit lower than expected, they emphasised that market players were already aware of a large drop in 1996 borrowing need.
"This was fairly well known...and although it was a slight positive surprise it does not change the overall picture," Nils Lundgren, Nordbanken chief economist, said.
Bond yields edged lower after the data was released. Nine-year bond yields fell three basis points to 6.79 from late on Wednesday after opening a basis point higher.
Economists were cautious over the debt office's forecast of a borrowing need of 20-30 billion crowns in 1997, saying it was hard to know exactly what the office based its estimates on.
"It is unclear if, and in that case how much, (money from) privatisations the office has included in its forecast," an analyst said.
Other economists said it was hard to know how much stronger growth the figures were based on.
Some economists believed the office would lower its 1997 forecast at some point.
"I would not be surprised if the forecast is lowered later (this year)," said Hansson at Handelsbanken. "1997 will be better than 1996 which saw growth of around 1.5 percent.

"Even if the Debt Office has based its forecast on (national economic research institute) KI's 1997 growth estimates, a rebound in private consumption could mean lower borrowing requirements in 1997."
Hansson said the Debt Office tended to be conservative in its forecasts.
But one analyst had another view.
"The office can be too optimistic when the situation looks brighter and too pessimistic when things are going downhill," the analyst said.
The debt office forecast the borrowing need for February at minus 9.8 billion crowns and lifted its January forecast to two billion crowns from a previous forecast of zero.
